value.overview: The Buffy Tuftedcheek (Pseudocolaptes lawrencii), also called Lawrence’s Tuftedcheek, is a distinctive furnariid of the highlands of Costa Rica and western Panama. It is a medium-sized, forest-dwelling bird associated with humid mountain environments. Its long rufous tail, buff cheek tufts, patterned head, and pale throat make it recognizable in the cloud forest. The species often searches moss, bark, bromeliads, and other epiphytes for animal prey.
value.classification: The Buffy Tuftedcheek belongs to the ovenbird family Furnariidae and the tuftedcheek genus Pseudocolaptes. It is a separate species from the Pacific Tuftedcheek and Streaked Tuftedcheek, with which it was formerly grouped by some taxonomic treatments.
value.identification: About 20 cm long, it has a brown back, olive-brown underparts, a spotted or streaked breast, dark wings with buff wingbars, and a long bright rufous tail. The crown is dark and buff-streaked, while the face shows a dusky eye stripe and conspicuous buffy cheek feathers. The throat is pale buff. Sexes are similar. It can be distinguished from other tuftedcheeks by its Central American range and combination of buff facial tufts and rufous tail.
value.rangeHabitat: The Buffy Tuftedcheek occurs from the central highlands of Costa Rica south through western Panama, reaching approximately Veraguas Province. In Costa Rica, it is a resident of the Central Highlands and the Cordillera de Talamanca, where it is found mainly in humid montane evergreen forest at roughly 1,550 m to timberline, near 3,000 m. It favors forest edges, natural openings, second-growth borders, and clearings containing scattered trees, as well as mature cloud forest with abundant mosses and epiphytes.
value.migrationStatus: Resident in Costa Rica and throughout its known range. It is not considered a regular long-distance migrant, although individuals may make local movements along mountain slopes or respond to changing conditions in high-elevation forests.
value.breeding: Reliable, species-specific information on breeding behavior and nesting details is limited. The species breeds within its montane range, including Costa Rica, and is believed to associate reproduction with humid highland forest habitats containing suitable moss-covered trunks, epiphytes, and natural cavities or sheltered sites. Precise nest structure, clutch size, incubation period, and parental care have not been sufficiently documented here.
value.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of arthropods, including insects and other small invertebrates, with small amphibians also reported as occasional prey. The Buffy Tuftedcheek commonly forages by inspecting moss, bark, lichens, bromeliads, and other epiphyte-covered surfaces. It may probe or pry into vegetation and crevices while moving through the middle and upper levels of humid mountain forest, often exploiting areas where epiphytes accumulate.
value.behavior: This species is an active but sometimes unobtrusive forest forager. It frequently moves through mossy branches and epiphyte-laden trunks, using its bill to search surfaces for concealed prey. Buffy Tuftedcheeks may occur singly, in pairs, or in mixed-species feeding groups. Their movements can be difficult to follow in dense cloud forest, but the bold facial pattern and rufous tail are conspicuous when the bird pauses in an opening.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not well quantified. Available assessments do not identify the species as currently meeting a threatened-category threshold.
